summary:
Lunar Landing Navigator is a desktop application that evaluates how suitable any point on the Moon is for landing, using real NASA satellite data. Users rotate an interactive 3D Moon and click a location. The app retrieves Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data (LOLA laser altimeter and Diviner radiometer) directly from NASA archives and scores the site from 0 to 100 on six criteria: surface slope, crater and rock density, sunlight, temperature, communication with Earth, and terrain.

Scoring uses published scientific methods and thresholds derived from Apollo and Artemis mission requirements. Separate mission profiles exist for robotic landers, crewed landings, lunar bases and rovers. A global heatmap colors the entire Moon by suitability, and 28 historic landing sites are shown for comparison.

As humanity returns to the Moon through Artemis, choosing a safe landing site is one of the most critical steps of any mission. Our project turns complex planetary data into a transparent, visual decision-support tool that students, researchers and mission planners can understand.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Lunar Landing Navigator is a desktop application that evaluates how suitable any point on the Moon is for landing, using real NASA satellite data.

The user rotates an interactive 3D Moon with the mouse and clicks a location. The application retrieves data directly from NASA’s Planetary Data System (PDS) archives. Instead of downloading multi-gigabyte files, it uses HTTP Range requests to read only the few megabytes covering the selected area. The site is then scored from 0 to 100 on six criteria:

  1. Surface slope: from the LOLA laser altimeter’s ~237 m elevation model, using Horn’s (1981) method.
  2. Crater and rock density: Diviner radiometer rock abundance map combined with automatic crater detection in LOLA data.
  3. Sunlight: solar geometry plus a 30 km terrain horizon profile.
  4. Temperature: radiative-equilibrium model for daytime, Diviner measurements for night.
  5. Communication with Earth: Earth’s elevation in the sky, including lunar libration and terrain horizon.
  6. Terrain: surface roughness and local relief.

The result is an overall score and a verdict (Highly suitable / Suitable / Conditionally suitable / Not suitable). The app also suggests the next date when the Sun will be at an ideal angle for landing. A global heatmap divides the Moon into about one million cells and colors the entire surface by suitability.

What are the benefits?

  • Transparency: every score shows which data and formula it came from; it is not a “black box”.
  • Mission-specific: separate profiles for robotic landers, crewed landings (Artemis), lunar bases and rovers. Changing the profile instantly re-scores everything.
  • Accessibility: turns complex planetary science data into a clear, visual tool, even for non-experts.
  • Comparison and reporting: analyzed sites can be compared side by side, and reports open in a browser and can be saved as PDF.

What is the intended impact?

As humanity returns to the Moon through the Artemis program, choosing a landing site is one of the most critical steps for mission safety. Our goals are:

  • to help students and young people learn planetary science by working with real NASA data,
  • to offer researchers and mission planners a fast pre-screening and decision-support tool,
  • to set an example of using scientific data in an open and verifiable way.

What tools and technologies did you use?

  • Language and platform: C#, .NET 8, Windows Forms
  • Development environment: Visual Studio 2022
  • External libraries: none. The 3D globe renderer, the PDS data reader and all calculations were written from scratch.
  • Data: NASA LRO LOLA (LDEM_4, 16, 64, 128), LRO Diviner GDR L3 rock abundance and nighttime temperature maps, NASA NSSDC landing coordinates
  • AI: an AI assistant (Claude) was used to support code development and research.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop; no special hardware required.

How creative is the project?

  • It scores the entire Moon with real data, according to mission type, and colors it on a rotatable 3D globe.
  • It uses a lightweight architecture that reads only the needed parts of huge NASA data files instead of downloading them.
  • Surface brightness follows the Lommel–Seeliger reflectance law used for the Moon. A “real Sun” mode shows the Moon’s current day–night boundary.
  • 28 real landing sites (Apollo, Luna, Chang’e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM and others) are shown on the globe and used to validate the algorithm.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific accuracy: thresholds come from real mission requirements: a 12° slope limit for the Apollo Lunar Module and 8–10° for the Artemis lander. Calculations use published methods, and results were checked against Diviner measurements. For example, the computed noon temperature at the equator is 386 K, while Diviner measures ~390 K.
  • Safety first: crater and rock density can only lower the score. Excessive slope, excessive rock, a fresh crater interior or no line of sight to Earth result in “Not suitable”, regardless of the average.
  • Honesty about limitations: resolution limits (~237 m for site analysis, ~2 km for the global map) and approximations (landing date ±12 hours) are clearly stated in the app. We emphasize that the weights are an engineering choice and that the score is a comparative, not absolute, measure.
  • User experience: a clean interface, a description next to every option, and a built-in user guide.
